taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO as Arbutus xalapensis Kunth. Arbutus texana Buckley is an older Texas name treated within this accepted concept.
look_here_first: Start with the bark: mature trunks and limbs shed thin outer layers to expose smooth cream, pink, apricot, orange, or red inner bark. Then confirm evergreen simple leaves, urn-shaped pale flowers, and orange-to-red berry-like fruit.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — Purola Preserve north Hays County natural-flora list includes Arbutus xalapensis among plants that occurred naturally, and a 2019 field collection independently recorded a wild Hays County plant. Bandera — 2019 UC Davis horticultural field collection documented a wild Bandera County tree. Real — the same field project documented a wild Real County tree in dense woodland.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Only explicit wild/natural target-zone county records were counted. Cultivated LBJ Wildflower Center records were excluded from county evidence.

best_field_traits: distinctive exfoliating bark revealing smooth pale cream, pink, apricot, orange, or red inner bark
clusters of pale urn- to bell-shaped flowers
Ericaceae-style anthers opening by apical pores
round fleshy berry-like fruit ripening from green through orange to red
Hill Country/West Texas rocky woodland and canyon association
morphology_keys.bark: The peeling, multicolored smooth bark is the fastest whole-plant recognition cue in mature Texas madrone.
morphology_keys.flower: Pale fused urceolate/campanulate flowers occur in clusters; inspect the stamens for the characteristic Ericaceae poricidal-anther pattern.
morphology_keys.fruit: Round fleshy fruits mature through orange/red and are eaten/dispersed by birds.
morphology_keys.ecology: Occurs naturally in rocky or canyon woodland settings; establishment can be associated with nurse-tree shade on the Edwards Plateau.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Texas madrone combines exfoliating multicolored smooth bark with evergreen leathery foliage, pale urn-shaped Ericaceae flowers, and orange-red berry-like fruit. Vaccinium arboreum lacks the dramatic madrone bark.
